title: How to Choose a Platform for Your Support Group
summary: Deciding where to host your group? What to look for in a platform, what each trade-off costs you, and the questions to ask before you commit.
body_markdown:
Most people choose a platform by picking the video tool they already have, then discover over the following months that the call was the easy part.


What actually determines whether an online group survives is everything around the call: how people find it, how they join, what reminds them, what exists between sessions, and what you can do when someone behaves badly at 8:40pm on a Tuesday.


## Start with the question nobody asks first


Not "which platform", but "what am I responsible for".


If you host the group yourself on a general video tool, you own the joining link, the member list, the reminders, the privacy settings, the moderation and whatever happens between sessions. All of that is doable. It is also several hours a month that you will not spend on the group itself.


If you use a platform built for groups, most of that is handled and you trade some control for it. Neither answer is wrong. Choosing without noticing you were choosing is what goes wrong.


## The nine things worth checking


What to check Why it matters How to test it


Joining on a phone Most members join from a phone. A difficult install loses people before session one. Join your own group from a phone you have never used it on.


Privacy controls A group that anyone can find or enter is not a support group. Try to find your own group while logged out.


Live moderation You need to mute or remove someone while the session is running, not afterward. Check the controls exist and that you know where they are.


Reminders The single biggest lever on attendance. Can you send one without giving out your personal number?


Between-session space Online groups vanish when the call ends. This is where members are lost. Is there anywhere for a member to post on a Thursday?


Accessibility Captions, phone dial-in, screen-reader support. Ask a member with a specific need to try it.


Your data if you leave Member lists and history are how a group survives a platform change. Ask, before you commit, how you export.


Payment, if you charge Chasing payments manually is what makes leaders quit. Check the fee structure and who handles refunds.


What it costs at scale Per-seat pricing punishes exactly the growth you want. Price it at 10, 30 and 60 members.


## The trade-offs, stated plainly


### General video tool


Cheap or free, familiar to everyone, excellent call quality. You do the rest: membership, reminders, privacy, moderation policy, and the between-session space. Best for a small group you already know, or a closed group running a fixed number of sessions.


### Purpose-built group platform


Membership, reminders, privacy and a persistent space are handled. You give up some control over the look and the flow, and you are dependent on somebody else's roadmap. Best for an ongoing group, a growing one, or a leader who is running more than one.


### Social platforms


Zero friction to start and enormous reach. But the privacy model is wrong for support groups, the platform decides what members see, and you are hosting sensitive conversations on infrastructure built for advertising. Good for finding people; poor for holding them.


### Clinical telehealth systems


Built for treatment, with the records and compliance apparatus that implies. If you are not delivering clinical care, this is the wrong tool and an expensive one, and using it can blur exactly the line between support and treatment you want kept clear.


## The privacy question, briefly


Most support group leaders are not covered entities under HIPAA, because HIPAA applies to healthcare providers, health plans and clearinghouses that transmit health information electronically for billing. Running a support group does not usually put you in that category.


That does not mean privacy is optional. What members tell each other is sensitive whether or not a federal statute names it, and the practical obligations are the same either way: control who gets in, do not record, do not keep more information than you need, and tell members what you do keep.


If you are a licensed clinician running a group as part of your practice, the analysis is different and you should check it against your own obligations rather than a general article.


## What changes as the group grows


Most platform regret arrives at about thirty members, not at five. The things that were fine when you knew everyone by name are the things that break.


- **Pricing that scales with headcount.** Per-seat pricing charges you more precisely as the group succeeds. Price any option at three times your current size before you commit, because that is the number you will be paying, not today's.
- **Moderation load.** At eight members you can read everything. At forty you cannot, and you need a way for members to flag something to you rather than relying on you noticing it.
- **More than one group.** The moment you run a second group, anything you were doing manually doubles. Reminders, membership, payments and joining links are the four that hurt first.
- **Handover.** If someone else ever co-facilitates or takes over, can they be given access without being given your password? A platform that has no concept of a second leader makes you the single point of failure.


None of this argues for the most featured option. It argues for asking what the group looks like in a year and choosing for that, because moving a running group between platforms costs you members.


## What you owe members either way


Whatever you choose, the obligations are the same and they do not depend on which statute applies to you.


Collect as little as you can. A support group needs a name and a way to contact someone. It does not need a diagnosis, a medical history or a date of birth, and every field you add is something you then have to protect.


Tell members what you keep, why, who can see it and how long you keep it. One short paragraph. Most leaders have never written this down, and writing it is usually the moment they notice they are holding more than they need.


Do not record sessions. The effect on what people are willing to say outweighs any benefit, and a stored recording of a sensitive conversation is a risk with no upside.


MentalHappy hosts expert-led psychoeducational support groups, supplemental to professional care, and does not sell, share, or distribute member information.


## Five questions to ask before you commit


1. Can a sixty-year-old member join from a phone, first time, without calling me?
2. If I have to remove someone mid-session, where is that button?
3. What happens in this group on a Thursday afternoon?
4. If I leave this platform in two years, what do I take with me?
5. What does this cost when the group is three times the size?


Run your own first session as a member, on a device you do not normally use, before you invite anyone. Most platform problems are visible in ten minutes and invisible from the host's seat.
